GK-11.c01: A **railroad-highway grade crossing** is where a road crosses tracks at the same level, and it is **always dangerous**.
Approach **every** crossing as if a train is coming, because a train's distance and speed are very hard to judge.
GK-11.c02: A **passive** crossing has **no traffic control device**, so the decision to cross is all yours.
An **active** crossing has flashing red lights (with or without bells), or lights with bells and **gates**, but you still must look.
GK-11.c03: The advance warning sign is **round, black on yellow**: slow down, look, listen, and be ready to stop.
All vehicles carrying **passengers or HazMat** must stop at railroad crossings.
The **crossbuck** means yield to the train; a sign under it shows the number of tracks.
With no white stop line, stop **no closer than 15 ft** and **no farther than 50 ft** from the nearest rail.
At gates, stop when the lights **start** flashing and stay stopped until the gates are **all the way up** and lights stop flashing.
GK-11.c04: **Never race a train**, and keep your speed low enough to **stop before the tracks** if needed.
Don't expect to hear a train or rely only on signals, gates or flaggers; always look yourself.
On **double tracks**, a train on one track can hide another, so check both ways after a train clears.
Yard and town or city crossings are **just as dangerous** as country crossings.
GK-11.c05: A **full stop** is required when your cargo makes it mandatory under state or federal rules, or when the law requires it.
When stopping, check traffic behind, stop **gradually** (use a pullout lane), and turn on your **4-way flashers**, since drivers behind may not expect it.
GK-11.c06: Never let traffic trap you on the tracks; be sure you can get **all the way** across before you start.
A typical tractor-trailer needs **at least 14 seconds** to clear a single track and **more than 15 seconds** for a double track.
**Don't change gears** while crossing the tracks, because a missed shift could stall you on them.
GK-11.c07: **Low-slung units** (lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, possum-belly livestock trailers) can hang up on raised crossings.
A **single-axle tractor** pulling a long trailer with landing gear set for a tandem-axle tractor can also hang up.
If stuck, **leave the vehicle and get well away** from the tracks, then call 9-1-1 and give the crossing's **DOT number** if posted.
GK-11.c08: In the mountains **gravity** is the big factor: it slows you going up and speeds you up going down.
Going down, choose a **safe speed**, use a **low gear**, and use proper braking so brakes hold you without overheating.
**Brake fade** means hot brakes need more and more pedal pressure for the same stopping power, until they may not stop you at all.
GK-11.c09: Your safe downhill speed depends on **five factors**: total weight, grade length, grade steepness, road conditions, and weather.
Never exceed a posted speed limit or **"Maximum Safe Speed"** sign.
**Engine braking** is your main speed control, strongest near **governed rpm** in a lower gear; save the service brakes.
GK-11.c10: Shift into a low gear **before** you start down the grade.
Don't downshift after speed builds: you may not get into **any** gear and **lose all engine braking**.
Older trucks use the **same gear** down as up; modern trucks **may need a lower gear** going down than going up.
GK-11.c11: Too much heat from overusing the brakes instead of engine braking makes them **fade or fail**.
Brakes **out of adjustment** stop doing their share first, so the other brakes **overheat and fade**; check adjustment often.
GK-11.c12: Brakes are only a **supplement** to engine braking; get into the proper low gear first.
Brake firmly enough for a definite slowdown to about **5 mph below** your safe speed, then release; each application takes about **3 seconds**.
Example: safe speed **40 mph** → brake to 35 mph, release, let it return to 40, and repeat ("snub braking").
**Escape ramps** stop runaway vehicles with a long bed of **loose, soft material**, sometimes with an upgrade; know where they are.
